implementation_notes: The compile-time way to guarantee inlining: the body is instantiated in the caller's TU with concrete types, so it is inlined by construction and the arguments become constants the optimiser can fold. This is why template and header-only libraries outperform shared-library ones - at the cost of code size and compile time.
idiom_name: template function instantiated at the call site
code_sketch: template <class T> T clamp_add(T a, T b, T limit) { return a + b > limit ? limit : a + b; }
pitfalls: Binary size grows with every distinct instantiation.
An implicitly instantiated inline template can violate the ODR across shared-library boundaries.

variants.name: The inline keyword (hint + ODR)
variants.implementation_notes: The standard form. Permits the definition in multiple TUs (an ODR requirement that it be identical) and raises the inlining priority. The safe variant: apply it to small cross-boundary helpers and let the compiler's cost model decide.
variants.code_sketch: inline int clamp(int x, int lo, int hi) { return x < lo ? lo : (x > hi ? hi : x); }
pitfalls: ODR: every TU must see an identical definition.

variants.name: Forced inlining
variants.implementation_notes: Overrides the inliner budget. Use only for the one function the profile shows as call-overhead-bound, and re-measure the instruction footprint afterwards - exceeding the i-cache makes the loop slower than the call it replaced. GCC errors if it cannot be inlined, which catches the impossible cases.
variants.code_sketch: __attribute__((always_inline)) static inline int step(int x) { return x < 0 ? 0 : x; }
pitfalls: Code size multiplies at every call site.
Can exceed the i-cache and lose.
